India captain Shubman Gill has questioned the continued prohibition on using saliva to shine the ball , arguing that it further tilts the balance towards batters, particularly when pitches offer little assistance.
Gill’s remarks came after India’s first Test against New Zealand at Basin Reserve ended in a draw on Monday, with the hosts batting out the final day to finish at 239 for five.
“I don’t understand why we haven’t been allowed to shine the ball yet. We are way past COVID times. There was a rule that you can’t put saliva on the ball to make it shine. It’s been seven to eight years, and I still don’t understand why they are not allowing it. I think this is also a big factor,” Gill said.
Fielding sides traditionally relied on saliva to maintain one side of the ball’s shine and help generate swing. The practice has been prohibited since the pandemic hit the world.
Gill felt the ball’s durability had become a concern, drawing parallels with India’s experience in England last year, where the Dukes ball too appeared to lose its hardness and shine earlier than expected.
“Ball definitely plays a big role. Our first ball (Kookaburra in NZ) was very soft after 25-30 overs. The other team also complained. We saw this in England (in 2025) as well. In the first three or four matches, the (Dukes) ball was getting soft very quickly. I don’t know if the quality of the balls has come down,” Gill said.
New Zealand captain Tom Latham, however, was less convinced that the saliva ban was necessarily up for reconsideration, pointing out that teams had to adapt to the regulations in place.
“Certainly, from a saliva point of view, I am not sure that will change, obviously, what the world’s been through, but again, you have got to find a way,” Latham said.
He acknowledged that the conditions at Basin Reserve and the ball’s inability to retain its characteristics for long had limited the bowlers’ opportunities.
“In the current day and age and the rules that we currently have, we work as hard as we can to keep the ball in as good a condition as possible from a swing point of view, but I think obviously conditions dictated that it didn’t necessarily last for long periods of time,” Latham said.
